segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was going out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, look! What stones and what buildings!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do you see these great buildings? Not one stone will be left here on another that will not be thrown down.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was sitting on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter, James, John and Andrew asked him privately,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus began to say to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Watch out that no one leads you astray.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he,’ and they will lead many astray.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: When you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. It must happen, but the end is not yet.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For nation will rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom; there will be earthquakes in various places; there will be famines. These things are the beginning of birth pains.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: As for you, watch out for yourselves. They will hand you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings because of me, as a testimony to them.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And the good news must first be proclaimed to all the nations.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: When they lead you away to hand you over, do not worry beforehand about what you will say, but say whatever is given to you in that hour, for it is not you who are speaking but the Holy Spirit.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Brother will hand over brother to death, and a father his child, and children will rise up against parents and put them to death.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And you will be hated by everyone because of my name. But the one who endures to the end will be saved.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But when you see the abomination that brings desolation standing where he should not be

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: (let the reader understand),

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: then those in Judea must flee to the mountains;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: the one on the housetop must not come down or go inside to take anything out of his house,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and the one in the field must not turn back to get his cloak.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Woe to those who are pregnant and those who are nursing in those days!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Pray that it may not happen in winter.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For those days will be a distress such as has not been from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, and never will be.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if the Lord had not cut short the days, no human being would have been saved. But for the sake of the chosen ones whom he chose, he has cut short the days.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Messiah!’ or ‘Look, there!’ do not believe it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For false messiahs and false prophets will arise and will give signs and wonders in order to lead astray, if possible, the chosen ones.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But you, watch out. I have told you everything beforehand.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But in those days, after that distress, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and the stars will be falling from the sky, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And then he will send out the angels and gather the chosen ones from the four winds, from the end of the earth to the end of heaven.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Learn the parable from the fig tree: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So you too, when you see these things happening, know that he is near, at the very doors.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But about that day or the hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Watch out, stay alert, for you do not know when the time is.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: It is like a man away on a journey, who left his house and gave his slaves authority, to each his work, and commanded the doorkeeper to stay awake.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So stay awake, for you do not know when the master of the house is coming, whether in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or early in the morning,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: or he may come suddenly and find you sleeping.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And what I say to you I say to everyone: Stay awake.”

notes.note: The Greek is simply 'I am' (egō eimi), the ordinary way to say 'It is I' or 'I am the one.' Here it most naturally means a claim to be the Messiah, as Matthew's parallel makes explicit. Some interpreters hear an echo of the divine self-designation 'I am' from the Greek Old Testament, but the context of impostors coming 'in my name' favours the simpler sense.

The Greek word was an ordinary term for the public announcement of good news, used also of royal and imperial proclamations. 'Gospel' now sounds like a religious term or a book title, so the plainer rendering is used. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

The phrase comes from the book of Daniel (9:27; 11:31; 12:11), where it refers to something detestable to God that defiles the temple and leaves it desolate. 1 Maccabees 1:54 applies it to the pagan altar that Antiochus IV set up in the Jerusalem temple in 167 BC. Jesus's hearers would have understood a comparable desecration to come; what event is meant is disputed, with many connecting it to the Roman war of AD 66–70.

notes.traditional: standing where it ought not to be
notes.note: 'Abomination' is a neuter noun in Greek, but the participle 'standing' is masculine, a mismatch a Greek reader would notice. It suggests the abomination is thought of as a person, or as embodied in one, and the translation reflects that with 'he.' Most English versions smooth this to 'it.' Some scholars treat the masculine as loose grammar without significance.

This is usually taken as an aside by Mark to the person reading his book aloud to a congregation, flagging the veiled reference; it is labelled here as the narrator's words. It could instead be part of Jesus's speech, addressed to the reader of Daniel. Matthew's parallel, which names Daniel, can be read either way.

The Greek word is an ordinary term for pressure, suffering or hardship. 'Tribulation' is now archaic and has become a technical term in some end-time schemes, which reads more into the word than a first-century reader would have heard. The wording echoes Daniel 12:1.

The Greek is literally 'all flesh would not have been saved,' a Semitic idiom in which 'all flesh' means every living person. 'Saved' here means surviving the distress. Most modern translations render the idiom in a similar way.

notes.phrase: the chosen ones whom he chose
notes.note: The noun and the verb share the same root in Greek, and the repetition is deliberate. 'The elect' hides the wordplay and has become a theological term; 'chosen ones' is what the word ordinarily meant and is used throughout the chapter.

The Greek christos translates the Hebrew title 'Messiah,' the anointed king Israel expected. Here the word is plainly a title for a figure people are looking for, not a name for Jesus, so 'Messiah' is used. The 'false messiahs' of the next verse are correspondingly rendered. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

The language of verses 24–25 is drawn from the prophets, especially Isaiah 13:10 and 34:4, where the darkening of sun, moon and stars accompanies God's judgment on nations such as Babylon and Edom. Interpreters differ on whether Jesus uses it here for literal cosmic events at the end of the age, or, as the prophets often did, as imagery for a world-shaking act of divine judgment within history.

notes.phrase: the Son of Man coming in clouds
notes.note: The words allude to Daniel 7:13, where 'one like a son of man' comes with the clouds of heaven to God and is given everlasting dominion. Most interpreters take the verse as Jesus's return in glory. A minority reads it, with Daniel, as his vindication and enthronement, seen in the events of that generation.

notes.traditional: he is near / it is near
notes.note: The Greek has no expressed subject, so 'he is near' (the Son of Man) and 'it is near' (the end, or the event just described) are both possible. English versions are divided. 'He' is chosen because the image of someone standing at the doors suits a person and the Son of Man has just been mentioned.

In ordinary usage, and elsewhere in Mark, the phrase means the people alive at the time of speaking. Because that raises the question of how 'all these things' happened within their lifetime, other senses have been proposed, such as 'this race' or 'this kind of people,' or the generation that sees the signs. The plain sense is the one most scholars accept for the Greek, with disagreement about what 'all these things' covers.

Many manuscripts read 'stay alert and pray.' The words 'and pray' are absent from a few important early witnesses and from the SBLGNT text translated here; they may have been added under the influence of Mark 14:38.

The Greek word means a person owned by another, and ancient hearers understood it so; in a household like this one, slaves could be entrusted with considerable responsibility. 'Servants' softens the word. Several modern translations now use 'slave,' while others keep 'servant' to avoid association with modern race-based slavery.

notes.phrase: whether in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or early in the morning
notes.note: These are the popular names of the four watches into which the Roman system divided the night, each about three hours long, from sunset to sunrise. The master may return during any of them, so the doorkeeper cannot count on sleeping through part of the night.
